oil.summary: Crude staged a firm intraday bounce — WTI +2.24% to $70.79 and Brent +2.76% to $73.98 — after a fresh U.S.-Iran escalation rattled the ceasefire narrative, even as both benchmarks sit roughly 21% below their month-ago peaks. The 60-day US-Iran ceasefire had already dragged prices sharply lower on expectations of a supply surge, with Middle East output rebounding to 14.6–15 million bpd. Markets are now questioning whether that supply wave materialises, per today's analysis flagging the guarantee risk. Offsetting the bearish ceasefire tone, Ukraine continued striking Russian refineries — with Putin publicly admitting fuel shortages for the first time — while RBOB gasoline slipped 2.14% on the session, diverging from crude. The CME options market prices a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting, underlining the fragility of current price levels.
drivers: US-Iran 60-day ceasefire triggered a ~21% monthly crude selloff on expected supply surge, but ceasefire durability remains in doubt following weekend flare-ups
Ukrainian drone strikes ignited multiple Russian refineries; Putin acknowledged domestic fuel shortages for the first time, adding a supply-disruption counter-narrative
CME options imply 77% probability of an OPEC production cut at next meeting, signalling producer discomfort with sub-$75 Brent

gas.summary: Henry Hub softened modestly, falling 1.27% to $3.19/MMBtu, while European TTF surged 4.84% to €42.755/MWh — a sharp transatlantic divergence driven by renewed Hormuz anxiety and supply-chain stress. Pakistan's state LNG importer issued an emergency cargo tender after weekend Hormuz flare-ups, illustrating spot-market tightness among vulnerable importers. Gulf producers — Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Qatar — continued loading LNG despite attacks on two commercial vessels, keeping flows intact for now. Ukraine's strike on a Russian gas plant added to European jitters. On the structural side, Williams is reportedly in late-stage talks to acquire pipeline operator Mo- in a deal worth ~$5.5 billion, reflecting continued U.S. LNG infrastructure buildout. Australian gas exploration investment hit a 10-year high amid energy-security concerns.
drivers: TTF spiked 4.84% on renewed Hormuz tensions and Ukrainian strike on a Russian gas plant, while Henry Hub eased 1.27% on softer domestic sentiment
Pakistan issued an emergency LNG cargo tender post-weekend Hormuz escalation; Gulf producers continue loading despite vessel attacks
Williams reportedly near a ~$5.5bn pipeline acquisition, and Australian gas exploration hit a 10-year high, both reflecting structural LNG infrastructure expansion

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs slipped 1.49% to $74.855/EUA, extending a modest weekly decline of 2.78%, as lower crude prices and ceasefire-driven fuel expectations reduced near-term decarbonisation urgency. However, TTF's sharp 4.84% one-day jump introduces upward cost pressure on gas-fired generation, which could tighten the carbon-to-gas spread for power producers. The geopolitical backdrop remains turbulent: Iran's announcement of a $6 billion asset release from Qatar redraws Gulf power dynamics and tests the ceasefire's credibility. On the demand side, China's summer power surge is pulling LNG imports back toward last year's levels per Kpler data, adding load to global gas-linked power markets. The Philippines emerged as the world's top solar panel buyer since the Iran war began, signalling accelerating clean-power substitution in energy-insecure emerging markets.
drivers: EUAs fell 1.49% as the ceasefire-driven crude selloff dampened carbon market urgency, though TTF's 4.84% daily surge pressures gas-fired power generation economics
Iran's $6 billion Qatar asset release and fragile ceasefire dynamics keep geopolitical risk elevated, sustaining uncertainty over European energy supply costs
Philippines became the world's top solar panel buyer since the Iran war, while China's summer power demand is lifting LNG imports back to year-ago levels
